hook.situation: A weekend plan keeps changing: you may go with a friend, you also need to email a teacher, you only have one hour, and you can do nothing but study. The nouns are simple; the particles decide the relationships.
objectives: Choose the right particle for receiver, companion, possession, also, only, scarcity, surprising amount, and minimum option.
Contrast similar particles such as 만 vs 밖에 and 도 vs 이라도.
Build real weekend-plan sentences instead of memorizing particle labels.
hook.whyItMatters: Korean particles are small, but they carry the grammar that English often puts in word order or prepositions. 친구, 친구에게, 친구랑, 친구도, 친구만, and 친구의 all start from the same noun but tell different stories.

grammarNotes.title: 에게 / 한테 / 께 — to a person (께 = honorific)
grammarNotes.func: Marks the person who receives or is the target of an action: giving, sending, asking, telling, lending. English uses 'to (a person)'.

formTable.when: Neutral or written, after any person noun
Casual spoken, after any person noun

formTable.ex: 친구한테서 들었어요 (I heard it from a friend)

examples.en: I gave a gift to a friend.
examples.note: 친구 is the receiver of 주다, so the person-target 에게 fits.

examples.en: I lent a book to my younger sibling.
examples.note: 한테 is the everyday spoken choice in casual talk.

examples.en: I sent an email to the teacher.
examples.note: 께 raises the receiver and pairs naturally with the humble verb 드리다.

examples.en: I sent an email to the company.
examples.note: A place or organization takes 에, not 에게 — 에게 is only for people (and animals).

keyPoint.label: 에게/한테 vs 께
keyPoint.body: 에게 and 한테 mean the same thing (한테 just sounds more casual). 께 is the honorific version for a respected person and usually rides with humble verbs like 드리다 and 여쭤보다.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 께 is a tense [kk] sound, like the kk in 'bookkeeper' — 선생님께 is [seon-saeng-nim-kke], never a plain [g].

drill.instruction: Fill the blank with 에게/한테 or 께, then read the whole sentence aloud.
drill.model: 친구___ 선물을 줬어요. → 친구에게 선물을 줬어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English 'gave to the gift' is obviously wrong, but learners attach 에게 to whatever follows 'to'. 에게 marks only the person receiver; the thing given takes the object particle 을/를.

grammarNotes.title: 와/과 · 하고 · (이)랑 — and / with
grammarNotes.func: Links two nouns ('A and B') or marks the companion you do something with ('with A'). All three mean the same; they differ only in register.

formTable.ex: 책 → 책과 가방 (a book and a bag)

examples.en: I watch a movie with a friend.
examples.note: 친구 ends in a vowel, so 랑; casual speech prefers (이)랑.

examples.en: I went together with Minsu.
examples.note: 하고 plus 같이 makes the 'with / together' reading unmistakable.

examples.en: I bought coffee and water.
examples.note: 커피 ends in a vowel → 와; this sounds tidy and slightly written.

examples.en: I brought only a book and a bag.
examples.note: 책 ends in a consonant → 과; the linker comes before the next particle 만.

keyPoint.label: 와/과 vs 하고 vs (이)랑
keyPoint.body: Meaning is identical; register differs. 와/과 = neutral-to-written, 하고 = neutral spoken, (이)랑 = casual spoken. Add 같이 when you want 'with' to be clear over 'and'.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 과 after a consonant tenses: 책과 sounds like [chaek-kkwa]; 와 after a vowel stays light, 커피와 [keo-pi-wa].

drill.instruction: Choose 와/과 or (이)랑 to match the final sound, then read it aloud.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 와/과·하고·(이)랑 connect nouns, not actions. To join two verbs ('watch and eat'), use the connective -고, not these particles.

grammarNotes.title: 밖에 + negative — nothing but / only (and it's not enough)
grammarNotes.func: Marks a limit that always needs a negative predicate. It frames the amount as scarce or insufficient: 'nothing but X', 'only X (and that's all there is)'.

formTable.ex: 한 시간밖에 없어요 (I only have one hour)
물밖에 못 마셔요 (I can drink nothing but water)
공부밖에 안 해요 (I do nothing but study)

examples.en: I can do nothing but study.
examples.note: 못 supplies the required negative; 밖에 alone can't stand with a positive verb.

examples.en: I only have one hour.
examples.note: 없어요 carries the negative and signals the time feels too short.

examples.en: There's no way except this one.
examples.note: 밖에 plus 없어요 = a forced, no-other-choice frame.

examples.en: I can only drink water.
examples.note: 물 takes 밖에 with no extra particle, paired with 못.

keyPoint.label: 밖에 vs 만
keyPoint.body: Both translate as 'only', but 밖에 demands a negative predicate and feels scarce/insufficient (공부밖에 못 해요), while 만 is neutral and takes a positive verb (공부만 해요). If you see a positive verb, you need 만, not 밖에.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 밖에 links across the ㄲ: [ba-kke], so 공부밖에 is [gong-bu-ba-kke] and 한 시간밖에 is [han si-gan-ba-kke].

drill.instruction: Complete each sentence so the predicate is negative (못/안/없어요).

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Because English 'only' goes with positive verbs, learners drop the negative. 밖에 grammatically requires 못/안/없어요. If you want a plain positive 'only', switch to 만.

grammarNotes.title: (이)나 — as many as / or
grammarNotes.func: After a number or amount it adds 'surprisingly much' (as many as); between two nouns it offers a loose choice ('A or B'). This chapter centers on the 'as many as' use.

formTable.ex: 다섯 잔 → 다섯 잔이나 (as many as 5 cups)
세 개 → 세 개나 (as many as 3)
물이나 마실까요? (shall we just drink water or something?)

examples.en: As many as three questions are left.
examples.note: 개 ends in a vowel → 나; the speaker feels three is a lot.

examples.en: I drank as many as five cups of coffee.
examples.note: 잔 ends in a consonant → 이나; emphasizes the surprisingly high count.

examples.en: I waited a whole hour.
examples.note: 시간 ends in a consonant → 이나; the wait felt long.

examples.en: Give me coffee or water (either is fine).
examples.note: Here (이)나 means a loose 'or' between two acceptable options.

keyPoint.label: (이)나 vs 밖에
keyPoint.body: Both attach to amounts but pull opposite ways. 다섯 잔이나 = the amount feels big (more than expected); 다섯 잔밖에 못 마셨어요 = the amount feels small (less than wanted). 나 says 'wow, that much'; 밖에 says 'only that little'.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 이나/나 trigger no special tensing; just match the final sound: 개나 [gae-na], 잔이나 [jan-i-na].

drill.instruction: Add 이나 or 나 to the number to mean 'as many as'.
drill.model: 세 개 ___ 남았어요. → 세 개나 남았어요.

englishSpeakerPitfall.right: 세 개나 남았어요. / 세 개밖에 안 남았어요.
englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: Learners blend the two because both attach to numbers. Pick one stance: 나 = surprisingly many (positive verb), 밖에 = surprisingly few (negative verb). They cannot stack.

grammarNotes.title: (이)라도 — at least; even if only
grammarNotes.func: Offers a minimum or fallback option when the ideal one isn't available: 'at least X', 'even if only X', 'X if nothing else'.

formTable.ex: 물이라도 마실까요? (shall we at least drink some water?)
잠깐이라도 쉬세요 (rest, even for a moment)

examples.en: If you don't have time, at least drink some water.
examples.note: 물 is consonant-final → 이라도; water is the fallback when there's no time for more.

examples.en: Shall we at least grab a coffee?
examples.note: 커피 is vowel-final → 라도; offers coffee as a modest plan.

examples.en: Rest, even for just a moment.
examples.note: 잠깐 is consonant-final → 이라도; 'even a little' time is better than none.

examples.en: Let's at least take the bus (go by bus).
examples.note: 버스 is vowel-final → 라도; the bus is the second-best option.

keyPoint.label: (이)라도 vs 만
keyPoint.body: 만 picks X as the exclusive choice ('only X'); (이)라도 picks X as a settling-for second choice ('X if nothing better'). 물만 마셔요 = I drink only water (by choice); 물이라도 마셔요 = at least drink water (since there's nothing else).

grammarNotes.pronunciation: (이)라도 is light with no tensing; just link smoothly: 물이라도 [mu-ri-ra-do], 커피라도 [keo-pi-ra-do].

drill.instruction: Add 라도 or 이라도 to the noun to mean 'at least / if nothing else'.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: (이)라도 and 만 express opposite attitudes (settling vs. exclusive), so they don't stack. Choose 이라도 for 'at least, if nothing else' or 만 for 'only, by choice'.

grammarNotes.title: 의 — 's / of (noun-to-noun link)
grammarNotes.func: 의 links two nouns to show possession or relationship, like English "'s" or "of": 친구의 가방 (a friend's bag). In speech it is usually dropped (친구 가방), and 저의/나의 contract to 제/내.

formTable.ex: 친구의 책 (a friend's book) · 한국의 음식 (Korea's food)

examples.en: This is my friend's book.
examples.note: 친구 + 의 + 책 — the first noun owns the second.

examples.en: Where is my bag?
examples.note: 저의 contracts to 제 — the everyday way to say "my."

examples.en: I like Korean food.
examples.note: 의 links 한국 to 음식 ("of Korea").

examples.en: My sibling's room is really big.
examples.note: In speech the 의 is dropped — 동생 방 = 동생의 방.

keyPoint.label: Drop 의 in speech; contract 저의 → 제
keyPoint.body: Written Korean keeps 의 (친구의 책), but spoken Korean usually drops it (친구 책). The one place it survives is the contractions 제 (저의), 내 (나의), 네 (너의) — always say 제 책, not 저의 책 in conversation.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: The possessive particle 의 may be pronounced [의] or, very commonly in conversation, [에]: 친구의 → [친구의] or [친구에]. Inside a word, non-initial 의 may also be heard as [이] in permitted pronunciations. Treat [에] as a useful spoken option, not the only possible sound.

drill.instruction: Link the two nouns with 의 (or its contraction).
drill.model: (친구 / 책) → 친구의 책 · (저 / 가방) → 제 가방

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: In speech, 저의 always shrinks to 제. Say 제 가방 (my bag), not 저의 가방 — the full form sounds stiff and written.

grammarNotes.title: (으)로 — by means of / toward (direction)
grammarNotes.func: Marks how you do something (tool, means, transport) or which direction you head: 'by/with X', 'toward X'.

examples.en: I go to school by bus.
examples.note: 버스 is vowel-final → 로; (으)로 marks the means of transport.

examples.en: I ate with my hands.
examples.note: 손 is consonant-final → 으로; the hand is the means/tool.

examples.en: I transferred to the subway.
examples.note: 지하철 ends in ㄹ, so just 로 (no 으); pronounced [ji-ha-cheol-lo].

examples.en: Come this way.
examples.note: 이쪽 is consonant-final → 으로; here it marks direction, not means.

keyPoint.label: (으)로 vs 에 (destination)
keyPoint.body: 에 marks the exact destination you arrive at (학교에 가요 = go to school); (으)로 marks the direction you face or the means you use (학교로 가요 = head toward school; 버스로 가요 = go by bus). For transport and tools, always (으)로, never 에.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: After ㄹ the 로 doubles the ㄹ: 지하철로 is [ji-ha-cheol-lo], not [ji-ha-cheol-ro].

drill.instruction: Add 로 or 으로 to match the final sound, then read it aloud.

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: English uses 'by bus' / 'to school' with no particle clash, but in Korean the means takes (으)로 and the destination takes 에. Don't put 에 on the transport — 버스에 가요 would mean 'go onto the bus'.

grammarNotes.title: 마다 — every / each
grammarNotes.func: Attaches to a noun to mean 'every X' or 'each X', often for repeated times or all members of a group: 'every morning', 'each person'.

formTable.ex: 세 시간 → 세 시간마다 (every three hours)

examples.en: I drink coffee every morning.
examples.note: 아침 + 마다 = 'every morning'; no extra time particle is needed.

examples.en: I meet my friends every weekend.
examples.note: 마다 attaches straight to 주말; it already means 'every', so don't add 에.

examples.en: Each person thinks differently.
examples.note: 사람마다 = 'each/every person'; great for talking about variation.

examples.en: I take medicine every three hours.
examples.note: 마다 after a counted unit gives regular intervals.

keyPoint.label: 마다 vs 매-
keyPoint.body: 마다 is a particle stuck onto a noun (아침마다, 날마다). 매 is a prefix glued in front (매일 = every day, 매주 = every week). Both mean 'every', but 매 forms set words while 마다 attaches freely to almost any noun.

grammarNotes.pronunciation: 마다 is plain and light: 아침마다 [a-chim-ma-da], 주말마다 [ju-mal-ma-da]. No tensing or linking surprises.

drill.instruction: Add 마다 to the noun to mean 'every / each'.
drill.model: 아침 ___ 커피를 마셔요. → 아침마다 커피를 마셔요.
items: 세 시간 ___ 약을 먹어요. (every three hours)

englishSpeakerPitfall.explanation: 마다 already carries the 'at every' meaning, so adding the time particle 에 is redundant and wrong. Use 마다 alone — never 마다에.

exampleSentence.en: Are you also going to see a movie with a friend this weekend?
I also sent the teacher an email.
I gave a gift to a friend.
I also need to send the teacher an email.
I also need to return my friend's book.
Are you also going to see a movie?
As many as three exam questions are left.
As many as three questions are left.
I can do nothing but study.
Do you want to at least drink coffee?
Should I at least bring you water?
There is no way except this.
I gave a gift to a friend.

extendedVocabulary.english: to give/send humbly to someone respected

exampleSentence.en: I sent the teacher an email.

extendedDialogue.setting: Two friends negotiate a weekend plan while one person has study obligations.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Are you also going to see a movie with a friend this weekend?
lines.grammarNote: 친구랑 marks companionship; 영화도 adds another activity.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 아니요, 시험 문제가 세 개나 남아서 공부밖에 못 해요.
lines.romanization: aniyo, siheom munjega se gaena namaseo gongbubakke mot haeyo.
lines.en: No, as many as three exam questions are left, so I can only study.
lines.grammarNote: 세 개나 shows the amount feels large; 밖에 pairs with 못 해요.

lines.speaker: 민서
lines.en: Then do you want to at least drink coffee? Just one hour.
lines.grammarNote: 라도 offers a minimum option; 만 limits the time.

lines.speaker: 지훈
lines.ko: 좋아요. 선생님께 이메일도 보내드리고, 친구의 책도 돌려줘야 해요.
lines.romanization: joayo. seonsaengnimkke imeildo bonaedeurigo, chinguui chaekdo dollyeojwoya haeyo.
lines.en: Sounds good. I also need to send the teacher an email and return my friend's book.
lines.grammarNote: 께 marks the respected receiver; 의 marks possession; 도 adds tasks.

readingText.title: 주말 계획을 조사로 정리하기
readingText.body: 주말 계획을 말할 때는 명사보다 조사가 더 많은 정보를 줄 때가 있어요. 친구랑 영화를 보면 함께 가는 사람을 말하는 것이고, 영화도 본다고 하면 다른 일에 영화를 추가하는 거예요. 시험 문제가 세 개나 남았다고 하면 양이 많게 느껴지고, 공부밖에 못 한다고 하면 선택지가 거의 없다는 뜻이에요. 그래도 커피라도 마시자고 하면 완전한 약속은 아니지만 최소한 가능한 제안을 하는 거예요. 마지막으로 선생님께 이메일을 보내드리고 친구의 책을 돌려줘야 한다면, 께는 받는 사람의 높임, 의는 소유 관계를 보여 줘요.
readingText.bodyTranslation: When talking about weekend plans, particles often carry more information than the noun itself. 친구랑 tells who you go with, 영화도 adds a movie to other plans, 세 개나 shows the amount feels large, 공부밖에 못 해요 means the options are limited, 커피라도 offers a minimum plan, 께 marks a respected receiver, and 의 marks possession.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 공부밖에 못 해요에서 왜 못 해요가 필요해요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 밖에가 부정 표현과 함께 쓰여서 선택지가 제한된다는 뜻을 만들기 때문이에요.

comprehensionQuestions.question: 커피라도 마실래요?는 어떤 느낌이에요?
comprehensionQuestions.answer: 완전한 계획은 아니지만 최소한 커피라도 마시자는 제안이에요.

culturalNote.title: A small particle can change the social meaning
culturalNote.body: 선생님에게 이메일을 보냈어요 is grammatically possible, but 선생님께 이메일을 드렸어요 sounds more respectful because 께 and 드리다 work together. In everyday speech, Korean speakers also drop 의 often, but they keep particles like 께, 밖에, 만, and 도 when those particles carry important social or logical meaning.
culturalNote.tip: When a sentence feels wrong, do not only change the noun. Ask what relationship the particle is trying to mark: receiver, companion, possession, addition, limit, scarcity, large amount, or minimum option.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence correctly marks the teacher as a respected receiver?
inlineExercises.explanation: 께 marks a respected person receiving the action, and 드리다 matches the respectful tone.
밖에 needs a negative idea such as 못, 안, or 없어요.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'as many as three exam questions are left'?
inlineExercises.explanation: 이나/나 after a number shows the amount feels large or surprising.
라도 offers a minimum or fallback option.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which pair shows the difference between 만 and 밖에?
inlineExercises.explanation: 만 works with a positive predicate; 밖에 needs a negative predicate.
의 links 친구 to 책: the friend's book.

inlineExercises.prompt: 선생님___ 이메일을 보냈어요. (I sent an email to the teacher.)
inlineExercises.explanation: 께 respectfully marks the receiver of the email. 께서 would mark the teacher as a respected subject, and 를 would make the teacher a direct object.

inlineExercises.prompt: Build: 'I have only one hour, and it is not enough.'
inlineExercises.explanation: 밖에 must pair with a negative like 없어요. It sounds like the amount is limited or insufficient.

inlineExercises.prompt: Say: 'Would you like at least coffee?'
inlineExercises.explanation: (이)라도 offers a minimum acceptable option. 커피라도 sounds like coffee would be okay even if it is not ideal.

inlineExercises.prompt: Which sentence means “I only drink coffee” without the scarcity feeling?
inlineExercises.explanation: 만 simply limits the choice to coffee. 밖에 plus negative adds a stronger “nothing except” feeling.

bullets: 에게/한테/께 marks a person receiving an action: 친구에게 선물을 줬어요, 선생님께 이메일을 드렸어요.
와/과/하고/(이)랑 links nouns or marks companionship: 친구랑 영화 봐요.
밖에 needs a negative predicate: 공부밖에 못 해요, 한 시간밖에 없어요.
이나/나 after a number shows a surprisingly large amount: 세 개나, 다섯 잔이나.
이라도/라도 offers a minimum option: 커피라도, 잠깐이라도.
의 marks possession or noun-to-noun relation, while 도 and 만 add or limit focus.

writingTask.prompt: Write a short message about giving something to a friend and what you do each week, using several particles.
writingTask.hint: Use 에게/한테 (to a person), 하고/(이)랑 (with/and), 밖에 + negative (only), 마다 (every), and (으)로 (by means of).
writingTask.model: 저는 친구한테 선물을 줬어요. 주말마다 친구하고 커피를 마셔요. 그런데 오늘은 시간이 한 시간밖에 없어요. 그래서 버스로 빨리 가요.
writingTask.modelEn: I gave a gift to my friend. Every weekend I drink coffee with my friend. But today I only have one hour. So I go quickly by bus.

canDo: Mark the person who receives an action (친구한테 · 선생님께)
Link nouns or a companion with 'and/with' (친구하고 · 친구랑)
Use 밖에 + negative for 'only', and 마다 for 'every' (한 시간밖에 없어요 · 주말마다)
Show means or direction with (으)로 (버스로 가요)
